did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word shemittah comes from a root meaning “to release” or “let go.” In this chapter, the release especially concerns financial debts.
The word yiggosh is related to approaching and pressing; here it describes forcefully demanding a debt. The Torah asks lenders not to pressure their fellow Israelites during the sabbatical year.
The phrase “whatever he lacks” teaches that help should meet a person’s real needs, not necessarily give everyone the same amount. The verse also speaks of lending, not only of giving gifts.
The words “a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman” show that the law explicitly addresses both male and female servants. For both, the period of service was limited to six years.
The Exodus is presented here not only as a national event, but also as a reason to act morally toward people who lack freedom. Remembering slavery is meant to shape how people treat others.

Piercing the ear against the door was a public symbolic act marking the person’s choice to remain in the household after becoming eligible for freedom. The doorway made the decision visible and memorable.
In this context, mum means a physical defect that makes an animal unfit for sacrifice, such as blindness or lameness. It does not mean the animal may never be eaten; it means it may not be offered.
The prohibition against eating blood appears elsewhere in the Torah because blood is treated as a symbol of life. That is why it must be poured onto the ground rather than used as food.
